title: Anonymous case study template: one-day activation - what worked and what did not
excerpt: A portfolio proves that you have done work. A case study demonstrates process, measurement and lessons. Here is a template for an anonymous one-day activation case study that builds trust in Montenegro.
description: A portfolio proves that you have done work. A case study demonstrates process, measurement and lessons. Here is a template for an anonymous one-day activation case study that builds trust in Montenegro.
coverAlt: Reviewing activation results and a case study retrospective
segments: In our market, portfolios often look attractive but leave one essential question unanswered: does the team know how to deliver results, or just how to make things look good? A case study goes beyond a portfolio because it reveals your thinking - not only what you did, but why, how you measured it, what went wrong and how you improved.

That is especially important in Montenegro, where budgets can be limited and trust relies on specifics. Clients want confidence that you have a repeatable process, can organize a team, message and customer journey, and can explain outcomes clearly.

The good news is that case studies can be anonymous. You do not need to disclose the client name, locations can be generalized and images can be replaced with non-identifying footage. But the numbers and reasoning must be real. Invented or suspiciously perfect figures undermine trust.
Template: one-day activation (anonymous)
1) Objective
Explain the main goal in one sentence: leads, visits, sales, UGC or bookings. If there is a secondary goal, mention it briefly, but one must remain primary.
Example: the objective was to capture X leads in one day for an offer available over the next 48 hours, with a secondary objective of collecting remarketing content.
2) Setup

This is where readers learn most, because they see the structure. Briefly state the location and duration, whether it was indoors or outdoors, which time of day was selected and why. Describe the team size and roles: first contact, form or QR management and logistics. State the offer or benefit in one sentence and the CTA channel: QR, coupon, DM or form.

If a visual or prop was central to attracting attention, explain what it was and why you chose it. That demonstrates that the activation was a planned experience, not simply a team standing around distributing materials.
3) Activation journey

Describe the visitor's path in a few sentences that make the real-world experience clear. Who approaches first? What is the opening line? What is explained in ten seconds? What small commitment is requested? How does the conversation end?

A good journey features an attention-grabbing hook, a short explanation that works in a noisy setting, a ten-second action and a clear next step confirmed immediately. That is where an activation differs from a promotional day.
4) Numbers: minimal but honest

You do not need 25 metrics. You need a few figures tied to the goal: estimated footfall per hour or period, real interactions, QR scans or clicks, leads or DMs, redeemed coupons or bookings, and UGC posts or clips. If useful, calculate conversion rates: interaction to scan, scan to lead and lead to purchase.

Clients care about how the numbers connect, not only about big totals. The journey reveals friction. Many interactions but few scans suggest a weak CTA. Many scans but few leads suggest a problem with the form or offer. Leads without follow-up results suggest the process after activation is failing.
5) What worked

This section needs specifics, not self-praise. Three concrete examples are enough: which message resonated best, the sentence visitors understood immediately, which CTA format was easier (QR or DM), and what attracted attention - visual, sampling, small challenge, first-contact staff or position in the venue.
These are elements readers can adapt to their own events, which is what makes the case study useful.
6) What did not work
This part builds trust. Claiming everything was perfect sounds like advertising. Naming one or two genuine problems sounds like experience.

Describe the friction: a form that was too long, a bottleneck in the crowd, a poorly positioned QR code, inconsistent team scripts, an unclear benefit or a quiet time slot with low footfall. A single failure can teach more than ten successes because it shows you understand what can be improved.
7) Lessons and next steps

Offer three short lessons and one concrete change for next time: shorten the form, revise messaging, move the stand, add a runner during busy periods, adjust the benefit or start remarketing the next day.

The next step is what completes the case study: if you repeated the activation, what would you change and how should that affect results? The best case study does not boast; it explains the process and lessons.
A case study builds confidence because it shows how you think, not just what you did.
FAQ
Do I need to identify the client?
No. You can anonymize the client, but the process and numbers must be genuine or you risk losing trust.
Which number matters most?
The figure connecting the activation directly to the goal: leads, bookings or sales. Everything else provides context.
